reading.title: Shackleton and the Crew of the Endurance
reading.purpose: Read how an Antarctic expedition survived months on shifting sea ice.
paras: In 1914, Ernest Shackleton sailed south with twenty-seven crew members on the wooden ship Endurance. They planned to cross Antarctica on foot. Months later, thick sea ice locked around the hull and crushed the ship. The crew faced grave hardship, living in thin tents on drifting ice with bitter winds and low food. Help was far away, yet Shackleton kept his crew calm.

Life on the sea ice was precarious, unsteady and ready to break apart beneath their boots at any hour. When the ice split, the men launched three open boats toward barren Elephant Island. The trip was daunting, so harsh and dark that most crews would have lost hope. Shackleton stayed tenacious, holding firmly to one promise: he would bring every sailor home alive.

No ship passed near Elephant Island, so Shackleton chose five men to sail one small boat across eight hundred miles of stormy sea to South Georgia Island. Huge waves soaked the boat while the men stayed stoic, enduring wet clothes and frostbite without complaint. Their quiet fortitude, the inner strength to keep rowing and bailing through bitter cold, carried them to land in sixteen days.

Even on shore, steep glaciers blocked the way to the whaling camp. Shackleton and two men stayed defiant against the cold and climbed across icy peaks. Through it all, he was steadfast and selfless: he gave his own mittens to a freezing sailor and kept daily routines to guard hope. Months later, a rescue ship reached Elephant Island, and all twenty-eight men lived—a lasting triumph of grit and teamwork.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "precarious" most nearly means
choices: carefully planned ahead of time by skilled sailors
unsteady and likely to break apart or fail at any moment
completely empty of wind, snow, or freezing temperatures
famous across the world for winning a dangerous race
qs.why: Paragraph 2 restates precarious directly as "unsteady and ready to break apart beneath their boots at any hour."

qs.q: Which sentence gives a concrete example of Shackleton putting a crew member's needs ahead of his own?
choices: Even on shore, steep glaciers blocked the way to the whaling camp.
Through it all, he was steadfast and selfless: he gave his own mittens to a freezing sailor and kept daily routines to guard hope.
Months later, a rescue ship reached Elephant Island, and all twenty-eight men lived—a lasting triumph of grit and teamwork.
Help was far away, yet Shackleton kept his crew calm.
qs.why: This sentence names a specific selfless action: giving his own mittens to a freezing sailor.

ev.text: Through it all, he was steadfast and selfless: he gave his own mittens to a freezing sailor and kept daily routines to guard hope.

qs.q: Why did Shackleton sail a small boat to South Georgia Island instead of waiting on Elephant Island?
choices: No passing ships traveled near Elephant Island, so waiting there meant no rescue.
The crew had already finished crossing Antarctica on foot and needed a trophy.
South Georgia Island had warmer beaches where wooden ships could be rebuilt.
He wanted to leave the rest of the sailors behind while he finished the race.
qs.why: Paragraph 3 states that "no ship passed near Elephant Island," which forced Shackleton to sail for help.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this biography?
choices: Wooden ships should never be used to carry explorers into the icy Weddell Sea.
Shackleton's steady leadership and his crew's endurance saved every man after their ship sank.
Crossing steep glaciers on South Georgia Island was easier than sailing an open lifeboat.
Antarctic expeditions usually succeed only when crews carry extra tents and warm mittens.
qs.why: The reading follows the Endurance crew from the crushed ship to their full rescue, highlighting leadership and endurance.

clues.text: living in thin tents on drifting ice with bitter winds and low food
unsteady and ready to break apart beneath their boots at any hour
enduring wet clothes and frostbite without complaint
the inner strength to keep rowing and bailing through bitter cold
